qs.q: (Exercise 4-178) The life of a semiconductor laser at a constant power is a lognormal random variable with a mean of 7104.26 hours and a standard deviation of 790.33 hours. What is the life in hours that 99.9$\%$ of the lasers exceed? Note: Round your final answer to the nearest whole hour.
hints: This is a lognormal percentile problem: the logarithm of the life is normal.
First convert the given mean and standard deviation of $X$ into the parameters $\theta$ and $\omega$ of $\ln X$, then find the 0.1th percentile of the normal variable $\ln X$.

For lognormal $X$: $E(X)=e^{\theta+\omega^2/2}$ and $V(X)=e^{2\theta+\omega^2}(e^{\omega^2}-1)$, so $\omega^2=\ln\left(1+\sigma^2/\mu^2\right)$; and $P(X>x)=p$ means $\ln x=\theta+z\,\omega$ where $P(Z>z)=p$ (here $z$ is negative when $p>0.5$).

qs.q: (Exercise 4-131) The life (in hours) of a magnetic resonance imaging machine (MRI) is modeled by a Weibull distribution with parameters $\beta=0.5$ and $\delta=1200$ hours. Determine the probability that the MRI fails before 4800 hours.
hints: This is a Weibull cumulative probability.
Identify the shape $\beta$ and scale $\delta$ and evaluate the Weibull cdf at the given time.
For a Weibull variable with shape $\beta$ and scale $\delta$: $F(x)=P(X\le x)=1-e^{-(x/\delta)^{\beta}}$ for $x>0$.

qs.q: (Suggested Problem 4-102) The distance between major cracks in a highway follows an exponential distribution with a mean of 12 km. What is the probability that the first major crack occurs between 24 and 36 km of the start of inspection?
hints: This is an exponential probability over an interval.
Find the rate from the mean, then subtract the survival (or cdf) values at the two endpoints.
If $X$ is exponential with mean $1/\lambda$, then $P(X>x)=e^{-\lambda x}$ and $P(a<X<b)=e^{-\lambda a}-e^{-\lambda b}$.

qs.q: (Suggested Problem 4-62) The fill volume of an automated filling machine used for filling cans of carbonated beverage is normally distributed with a mean of 355 cc and a standard deviation of 5 cc. What is the probability that a fill volume is exactly 345 cc?
hints: Think about what the probability of a single exact value means for a continuous random variable.
The fill volume is continuous, so ask how much area lies under the density curve over a single point.
For a continuous random variable $X$ and any number $c$: $P(X=c)=\int_c^c f(x)\,dx=0$.
steps: The values 0.02275 and 0.97725 would be $P(X<345)$ and $P(X>345)$, which are different questions.

hints: This is a probability from a density function, so integrate the density.
Integrate $f(x)$ over the interval from $-0.5$ to $0.5$.
For a pdf $f$: $P(a<X<b)=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$, and $\int x^n\,dx=\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}$.

qs.q: (Exercise 4-23) The gap width is an important property of a magnetic recording head. In coded units, if the width is a continuous random variable over the range $0<x<4$ with $f(x)=0.125x$, determine the cumulative distribution function of the gap width.
hints: The cdf is obtained by accumulating the density from the left end of the range.
Integrate $f(t)$ from the lower end of the range up to $x$, and remember the cdf is 0 below the range and 1 above it.
$F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}f(t)\,dt$, and $F(x)=1$ once $x$ reaches the upper end of the range.
steps: $F(x)=0$ for $x\le0$, which gives the piecewise function with $0.0625x^2$ on $0<x<4$.

qs.q: (Exercise 7-4) Suppose that samples of size $n=5$ are selected at random from a normal population with mean 120 and standard deviation 12. What can you say about the probability that the sample mean falls in the interval from $\mu_{\bar X}-1.73\,\sigma_{\bar X}$ to $\mu_{\bar X}+0.95\,\sigma_{\bar X}$?
opts: This probability cannot be found because the sample size is small.
hints: The population is normal, so the sample mean is exactly normal for any sample size.
Standardize: the interval endpoints are already given in units of $\sigma_{\bar X}$ from the mean, so they are the $z$ values.
If the population is normal, $\bar X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)$ exactly and $Z=\dfrac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim N(0,1)$.
steps: Since the population is normal, $\bar X$ is normal for any $n$, with $\mu_{\bar X}=120$ and $\sigma_{\bar X}=12/\sqrt5$.

qs.q: (Exercise 7-12) The amount of time that a customer spends waiting at an airport check-in counter is a random variable with mean 8.5 minutes and standard deviation 6 minutes. Suppose that a random sample of $n=58$ customers is observed. Find the probability that the average time waiting in line for these customers is more than 10.1 minutes.
hints: The sample is large, so use the central limit theorem for the sample mean.
Standardize 10.1 using the mean and standard error of $\bar X$, then take an upper-tail probability.
By the CLT, for large $n$, $\bar X$ is approximately $N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)$, so $Z=\dfrac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$ is approximately standard normal.

qs.q: (Exercise 8-9) Suppose that $n=100$ random samples of water from a freshwater lake are taken and calcium concentration (mg/L) measured. A 95$\%$ confidence interval on the mean calcium concentration is $[0.52,\ 0.74]$. Which interpretation of this interval is correct?
opts: If we were to repeat this entire sampling process many times (taking $n=100$ samples and computing a 95$\%$ CI), about 95$\%$ of those intervals would contain the true mean $\mu$.
There is a 95$\%$ probability that the true mean calcium concentration $\mu$ lies between 0.52 and 0.74 mg/L.
About 95$\%$ of individual water samples from this lake have calcium concentration between 0.52 and 0.74 mg/L.
Because the confidence level is 95$\%$, at least 95 of the 100 measured samples in this study must lie between 0.52 and 0.74 mg/L.
With 95$\%$ confidence, the calcium concentration of the next single water sample drawn from this lake will lie between 0.52 and 0.74 mg/L.
hints: This is about the meaning of a confidence level.
Ask what is random: the interval (it changes from sample to sample) or the fixed true mean.

A $100(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence level is the long-run proportion of intervals, built the same way from repeated samples, that contain the fixed parameter; it is not a probability statement about one computed interval, and not about individual observations.
steps: The true mean $\mu$ is a fixed number, and the interval depends on the random sample.
The 95$\%$ describes the method: in repeated sampling, about 95$\%$ of the intervals formed this way capture $\mu$.
The interval is for the mean, not for individual measurements, so the statements about individual samples or the next sample are wrong.
A given computed interval either contains $\mu$ or not, so a 95$\%$ probability statement about it is not correct. Only the repeated-sampling statement is correct.
qs.brief: CI level = long-run proportion of such intervals that contain $\mu$.

qs.q: (Exercise 8-7) A confidence interval estimate is desired for the gain in a circuit of semiconductor device. Assume that the gain is normally distributed with the standard deviation $\sigma=30$. How large $n$ must be if the length of the 95$\%$ confidence interval is to be 30?
hints: This is a sample size problem for a mean with known $\sigma$.
The length of the interval is twice the margin of error; set it equal to the required length and solve for $n$.
The length is $L=2z_{\alpha/2}\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$, so $n=\left(\dfrac{2z_{\alpha/2}\sigma}{L}\right)^2$, rounded up.

qs.q: (Exercise 8-14) The lifetime in hours of 75-watt light bulbs is known to be normally distributed with standard deviation of 25 hours. A random sample of size 20 bulbs has a mean life of 1014 hours. The margin of error for a 78.87$\%$ confidence interval on the mean lifetime is
hints: This is a confidence interval for a mean with known $\sigma$; the question asks for the margin of error only.
Find the $z$ value that leaves $\alpha/2$ in each tail for the given confidence level, then multiply by the standard error.
Margin of error $E=z_{\alpha/2}\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$, where $\alpha=1-\text{confidence level}$.

qs.q: (Exercise 8-60) A study is to be conducted of the percentage of homeowners who own at least two television sets. How large a sample is required if we wish to be 97$\%$ confident that the error in estimating this percentage is less than 0.017?
hints: This is a sample size problem for a proportion with no prior estimate of $p$.
Since no estimate of $p$ is given, use the value of $p$ that makes the required $n$ largest (the conservative choice).
$n=\left(\dfrac{z_{\alpha/2}}{E}\right)^2p(1-p)$, which is largest at $p=0.5$, giving $n=0.25\left(\dfrac{z_{\alpha/2}}{E}\right)^2$, rounded up.

qs.q: (Exercise 8-1(c)) For a normal population with known variance, the confidence level for the interval $\bar x\pm1.85\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$ is
hints: Reverse the usual confidence interval construction: find the confidence level from the $z$ multiplier.
The multiplier 1.85 is $z_{\alpha/2}$; find the area between $-1.85$ and $1.85$ under the standard normal curve.
The confidence level is $1-\alpha=P(-z_{\alpha/2}<Z<z_{\alpha/2})=2\Phi(z_{\alpha/2})-1$.

qs.q: (Exercise 8-27 modified) A research engineer for a tire manufacturer is investigating tire life for a new rubber compound and has build 16 tires and tested them to end-of-life in a road test. The sample mean is $\bar x$ km and the sample standard deviation is $s$ km. A 90$\%$ confidence interval on the mean tire life is reported as $[5514.28,\ 60284.91]$. What is the value of the sample standard deviation $s$?
hints: This is a t confidence interval for the mean (unknown $\sigma$), worked backwards.
The margin of error is half the width of the interval; equate it to $t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\,s/\sqrt n$ and solve for $s$.
The interval is $\bar x\pm t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\dfrac{s}{\sqrt n}$, so $s=\dfrac{E\sqrt n}{t_{\alpha/2,n-1}}$ with $E=\dfrac{\text{upper}-\text{lower}}{2}$.
